id: Anna May Wong Stars as Cyborg #86

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The future is as sterile as a robot’s loincloth. I drown my hands in sanitizer until they pucker. Where this soapbox tree germinates, I collect my germs and make a fountain of them. Because yellow is yarrow and soot, and the future, I’ve learned, is no suture. Because where I’m from, these kisses are infections. Because dirt’s ammunition against discipline, the blood fills my clean mouth with dismay. Am I surprised— Hollywood still assumes we are all the bastard children of the same evil dictator? That phosgene and mustard will rack our titanium Maoist husks until some white man with slanty eyes rescues us from our mealy, pliant selves? Am I to wear Dior, wrap my mouth in bloody tulle, before kneeling, bending to kiss a mouth dirtied by Pantone 136? No fucking thanks. Because where I’m from, these kisses are infractions. Darlings, let’s rewrite the script. Let’s hijack the narrative, steer the story ourselves. There’d be a heist, a battle. Audre Lorde would write the script. My leading man would be Bruce. We’d earn our happy ending. Instead, they give me 1981. 2012. Quantum quasars, new dystopia—plutonium wars. We’re not in Polanski’s Chinatown anymore. Yet we still have the same bowl haircuts. Bangs, big bang, a city of fetid promise, new minor galaxy where we cannot touch. Instead our skin is rust and metal. It gratifies the technophile in all of us.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Where, Because

outputs.L1:
The future is as sterile as a robot’s loincloth. I drown my hands in sanitizer until they pucker. Where this soapbox tree germinates, I gather my germs and make of them a fountain. Because yellow is yarrow and soot, and the future, I have learned, is no suture. Because where I come from, these kisses are infections. Because dirt is ammunition against discipline, the blood fills my clean mouth with dismay.

Am I surprised that Hollywood still assumes we are all the bastard children of the same evil dictator? That phosgene and mustard will rack our titanium Maoist husks until some white man with slanty eyes rescues us from our mealy, pliant selves? Am I meant to wear Dior, wrap my mouth in bloody tulle, then kneel and bend to kiss a mouth dirtied by Pantone 136? No fucking thanks.

Because where I come from, these kisses are infractions.

Darlings, let us rewrite the script. Let us hijack the narrative and steer the story ourselves. There would be a heist, a battle. Audre Lorde would write the script. My leading man would be Bruce. We would earn our happy ending.

Instead, they give me 1981. 2012. Quantum quasars, a new dystopia—plutonium wars. We are not in Polanski’s *Chinatown* anymore. Yet we still have the same bowl haircuts. Bangs, big bang: a city of fetid promise, a new minor galaxy where we cannot touch. Instead, our skin is rust and metal. It gratifies the technophile in all of us.
outputs.L2:
The future has the antiseptic blankness of a robot’s loincloth. I soak my hands in disinfectant until the skin wrinkles. Wherever this pulpit-tree takes root, I gather up my microbes and turn them into a fountain. Since yellow means yarrow, soot, and what comes next—and I have discovered that the future stitches nothing closed. Since, in the place I come from, kisses like these count as contagions. Since dirt arms itself against order, blood floods my scrubbed mouth with dread.

Should I be shocked that Hollywood still imagines us as the illegitimate offspring of one shared tyrant? That phosgene and mustard gas will torture our titanium Maoist shells until a white man with slanted eyes arrives to save us from our soft, grainy compliance? Am I supposed to put on Dior, veil my mouth in blood-soaked tulle, then kneel and lean forward to kiss lips stained with Pantone 136? Absolutely fucking not.

Because where I come from, kisses like these are violations.

Beloveds, let’s revise the screenplay. Let’s seize the plot and drive the story on our own terms. There would be a robbery, a war. Audre Lorde would be the one to write it. Bruce would play my romantic lead. We would win our happy ending ourselves.

But instead they hand me 1981. They hand me 2012. Quantum quasars, another dystopia—wars of plutonium. We are no longer inside Polanski’s *Chinatown*. Still, somehow, the bowl cuts remain. Bangs, the big bang, a city rank with possibility, a small new galaxy where touch is forbidden. In its place, our bodies become corrosion and machinery. It pleases the technophile hidden in each of us.
outputs.L3:
The speaker rejects a sterile and sanitized vision of the future, one in which human contact, dirt, sweat, and intimacy are treated as forms of contamination. This imagined future appears clean and technologically advanced, but it is also emotionally empty and hostile to the body. By refusing this version of progress, the speaker insists on the value of touch, physical presence, and the messy realities of human life.

At the same time, the text criticizes racist Hollywood narratives that have long portrayed Asian people through stereotype, spectacle, and violence. These stories often reduce Asian characters to exotic figures, victims, villains, or background bodies, while positioning white protagonists as rescuers or heroes. The speaker exposes how these narratives distort reality and deny Asian people full humanity, agency, and complexity.

The speaker also refuses to perform the roles imposed by fashion, film, and cultural expectation. They reject being made into an exotic object, a submissive figure, or a decorative symbol designed for someone else’s gaze. Instead of accepting these limited identities, the speaker challenges the systems that produce them and refuses to be shaped by fantasies rooted in racism and fetishization.

A central demand of the text is that marginalized people reclaim the power to tell their own stories. Rather than being written by dominant cultures, they must become the authors of their own narratives. The speaker imagines a story defined not by victimhood or imposed stereotypes, but by self-direction, struggle, survival, and victory. This act of rewriting becomes a form of resistance and liberation.

The poem also contrasts futuristic dystopian imagery with the persistence of old racist stereotypes. Even in a world of advanced technology, the same patterns of exclusion, alienation, and racial violence remain. This contrast suggests that technological progress alone does not create justice. A society may appear modern or futuristic while still carrying the prejudices of the past. The speaker therefore challenges both the fantasy of a clean, perfected future and the cultural narratives that continue to dehumanize marginalized people.
outputs.L4:
The speaker critiques the sterile futures often imagined in dystopian science fiction, especially those shaped by Hollywood’s racial fantasies and fears. In these worlds, the future is sleek, metallic, controlled, and emotionally empty. Bodies are often treated as objects, machines, threats, or surfaces onto which anxiety is projected. The poem challenges this vision by focusing on how Asian bodies have been represented in film and popular culture: as artificial, exotic, disposable, dangerous, or untouchable. Rather than accepting these images as neutral entertainment, the speaker exposes them as part of a larger pattern of dehumanization.

Through visceral imagery, repetition, and cinematic references, the poem shows how touch, identity, and desire become distorted by racism. Physical contact is framed not as intimacy or connection, but as contamination, invasion, or control. The Asian body is imagined as something to be feared, consumed, disciplined, or erased. By returning again and again to images of metal, skin, machinery, and performance, the speaker emphasizes how these representations turn living people into symbols or props. The repetition creates a sense of pressure, as if the same harmful scripts keep being replayed across different movies, genres, and historical moments.

At the same time, the poem refuses to remain trapped inside these inherited narratives. Its use of film language suggests that representation is constructed: scenes are written, roles are assigned, bodies are staged, and endings are chosen. Because these images are made, they can also be remade. The speaker recognizes that resisting racist representation requires more than simply criticizing old stories; it also requires imagining new ones. New scripts, new heroes, and new endings become forms of survival and rebellion.

The poem ultimately argues that reclaiming the narrative is essential. Against futures that are cold, metallic, and untouchable, the speaker insists on a future shaped by self-definition, embodied experience, and human connection. By exposing the violence behind familiar cinematic tropes, the poem opens space for different forms of desire, identity, and belonging. Its conclusion is not merely a rejection of dehumanizing images, but a demand for representation that allows Asian bodies and voices to exist fully, complexly, and on their own terms.
outputs.L5:
**The Where Because**

The word **“the”** points to something specific. It gives shape to a thought, turning any place or thing into something known: *the road, the sky, the moment*.  

**“Where”** asks for direction. It is a word of curiosity, used when we search for a place, an answer, or even a purpose: *Where are we going? Where do we belong?*  

**“Because”** gives a reason. It connects actions to meaning and helps us understand why something happens: *We stayed because it was safe. We tried because we believed.*  

Together, these three words can form the beginning of a story: **The place where we met mattered because it changed everything.**

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, surreal prose poem in the voice of an Asian American speaker critiquing Hollywood Orientalism, sci-fi dystopias, hygiene, contagion, and racist rescue narratives; make it angry, lyrical, and full of strange imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
I was born in the subtitle, under the studio moon, where every Chinatown burns blue and obedient for the camera, where rain is a neon servant washing the same alley of its yellow peril. Hollywood keeps asking me to step from a paper lantern with a knife in my teeth or a virus in my blood, keeps mistaking my grandmother’s soup for a biohazard, her hands for evidence, her accent for fog. The future, they say, is always overpopulated, always damp, always speaking a language the hero cannot pronounce before he saves it with a gun and a clean white jaw.

I have seen your dystopias: cities stacked like infected teeth, markets steaming with engineered dread, masks blooming on faces like accusations. I have watched the camera crawl through bowls, cages, cables, bodies, searching for the origin of catastrophe in the broth of someone else’s dinner. The apocalypse arrives wearing my mother’s face and your panic calls it realism. You disinfect the plot with bleach and bullets. You name the cure after the colonizer. You scrub and scrub until the screen squeaks, until every brown hand becomes a smear, until the hero can kiss the ruined world without catching what he invented.

Do not rescue me. I know that helicopter: its blades are scissors cutting history into manageable scenes. I know that soldier with the tender eyes, entering the quarantine zone as if entering a womb he owns. He carries antibiotics, democracy, a child actress, and the old hunger to be forgiven by the people he has already framed as doomed. Behind him, the music swells like a police report trying to become a hymn.

My anger has six wings and a mouth full of mothballs. It lives in the laundry room with the hot pipes, in the nail salon’s acetone dawn, in the motel ice machine coughing up little translucent coffins. My anger wears nitrile gloves and still refuses to touch your script. It climbs the billboard, licks the white letters, turns them to salt. It says: your hygiene is not innocence. Your cleanliness has a border. Your fear of contagion is a chapel built from stolen breath.

Tonight I walk through the backlot city, past the fake temple, the fake noodle stall, the fake woman dying beautifully beneath a red umbrella. I unhook the moon from its rigging. I release the extras from their painted silence. We open every prop cabinet: plague masks, dragon robes, passports, severed braids, futuristic police helmets, vials of green doom. We grind them into powder and season the sky. The stars begin to sneeze. The hero develops a rash shaped like an empire.

And still my people are not metaphor. We are not the mist, not the market, not the warning flickering at the edge of the Western imagination. We are the hand that turns off the projector. We are the cough that speaks back. We are alive in the unclean, brilliant world, carrying our dead without becoming your disease, washing our bowls without asking to be purified, burning with a light no rescue can survive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental monologue that blends cyberpunk futurism, pandemic-era sanitation, Maoist imagery, chemical warfare references, and a rejection of white savior cinema, ending with a call to rewrite the narrative.
counterfactuals.output:
The city wakes under neon quarantine—  
a chrome lung coughing in violet light,  
its alleys rinsed nightly with disinfectant rain,  
bleach mist hissing from drones like mechanical cicadas.  

We learned to recognize each other by the eyes.  
By the tremor in a gloved hand.  
By the fog of breath trapped behind plastic shields.  
By the ritual: sanitize, scan, submit, survive.  

Every doorway became a checkpoint.  
Every body, a border.  
Every cough, a siren.  

Above us, billboards flicker with the Chairman’s face—  
not the man, but the icon: red sun, raised hand,  
a thousand copied profiles burned into LED haze.  
The old slogans return as software updates:  
serve the people, report the fever, optimize obedience.  
The revolution is livestreamed in thermal imaging.  
The village loudspeaker has become a citywide push notification.  

And somewhere beneath the asphalt, history leaks.  
Not clean history.  
Not museum history.  
A buried arsenal history—  
mustard-yellow ghosts, nerve-agent whispers,  
gas masks hanging like dead fruit in the memory of the century.  
The wars promised to end all wars  
only perfected the art of entering the body unseen.  
The future did not arrive as a flying car.  
It arrived as aerosol.  
As residue.  
As a protocol no one remembers voting for.  

They told us salvation would come in a white frame:  
a foreign lens, a gentle voiceover,  
a hero descending into our ruins with clean hands  
and a tragic soundtrack.  
They wanted our suffering color-graded,  
our dead translated into awards-season empathy,  
our mothers reduced to background grief,  
our streets turned into proof  
that someone else could feel human.  

No.  

No more white savior cinema.  
No more imported redemption.  
No more stories where we are atmosphere,  
where our revolutions are scenery,  
where our pain becomes the moral education of strangers.  

We are not the neon backdrop to your awakening.  
We are not the infected crowd parting for your cure.  
We are not the child you rescue so the audience can forgive you.  
We are not the red flag, the gas cloud, the quarantine tape,  
the exotic wound, the grateful survivor.  

We are the ones scrubbing the blood from the clinic floor.  
We are the ones welding antennas to rooftops.  
We are the ones printing pamphlets in basements  
while drones comb the sky for unauthorized hope.  
We are the ones who know that a mask can be protection,  
disguise, muzzle, banner.  

So let the old reels burn blue in the data fire.  
Let the subtitles crack.  
Let the hero shot collapse.  
Let the camera turn around.  

Give the microphone to the nurse with bleach-burned hands.  
Give the frame to the courier on the electric bike.  
Give the archive to the grandmother who survived one purge, two famines, three regimes,  
and still hides seeds in a tin beneath her bed.  
Give the final cut to the people who lived the scene.  

The future is not clean.  
The revolution is not cinematic.  
The plague was never just a plague.  
The war was never only over there.  
The story was never theirs to own.  

So tonight, under the red neon, beneath the sterilized rain,  
with history stinging in our lungs  
and the city pulsing like a hacked machine,  
we do not wait to be saved.  

We seize the lens.  
We break the script.  
We rewrite the narrative.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a politically charged prose poem inspired by Audre Lorde, Bruce Lee, and neo-noir films like Chinatown, using motifs of dirt, kisses, infection, metal bodies, and dystopian futures.
counterfactuals.output:
The city kept its files under the fingernails.

Every morning, the clerks washed and washed,  
but the dirt returned—  
black as a redacted name,  
sweet as oil beneath the tongue.  
In the ministries of tomorrow  
men with polished teeth declared the soil unclean,  
then sold it back to us by the acre,  
bagged and branded,  
with a flag stitched into the seam.

We learned to kiss like fugitives:  
quickly, in stairwells,  
against the blue pulse of police drones,  
mouths passing warmth like contraband.  
A kiss could be a wound,  
a cure,  
an infection of memory.  
Your lips said: *they want us sterile.*  
Mine answered: *then let us become contagious.*

At night the rain came down metallic,  
ticking on the roofs of the poor  
like a thousand tiny verdicts.  
The rich had upgraded their bodies—  
spines of chrome, lungs of glass,  
hearts humming behind locked plates.  
They did not bleed anymore.  
They leaked.  
They rusted in private.  
They hired children to polish them  
until they could see no future  
but their own reflection.

Somewhere in the old quarter  
a detective with tired eyes  
followed a trail of water  
to a room full of dust.  
The dust spoke first.  
It said: *every empire begins as a real estate scheme.*  
It said: *every map is a confession.*  
It said: *look what they buried to make the garden bloom.*

And beneath the garden—  
bones, cables, ballots, teeth.  
A whole century of bitten tongues.

We were told rage was a sickness.  
We were told tenderness was weakness.  
We were told our bodies were borders  
and borders were sacred  
and sacred meant guarded  
and guarded meant owned.

But the body remembers another law.

The fist knows the gate.  
The foot knows the wall.  
The breath, if kept low and burning,  
can move through cages  
as water moves through stone—  
patient, formless,  
ruining the architecture.

So we gathered in the contaminated dawn,  
women with dirt in our hair,  
men with kisses hidden in their palms,  
children whose metal knees sparked as they ran.  
We carried no purity.  
Purity belonged to laboratories,  
to prisons,  
to men who feared the world enough  
to bleach it.

We carried infection instead:  
songs that spread through checkpoints,  
names that multiplied on forbidden walls,  
love with its dangerous fever,  
grief with its black light,  
hope with its dirty hands.

The future stood before us  
in a coat of rain and neon,  
smoking beside a dead river.

It said, *You can’t win.*

We kissed it on the mouth.

And watched it catch fire.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fragmented, avant-garde piece about racialized representation in Hollywood science fiction, with references to Dior, Pantone yellow, mustard gas, titanium bodies, bowl haircuts, and forbidden touch.
counterfactuals.output:
**CHROMA KEY / MINORITY REPORT**

Hollywood makes the future  
and calls it neutral.

A white room.  
A white ship.  
A white helmet gleaming like a doctrine.

Then—  
a body of color enters frame  
as atmosphere,  
as omen,  
as best friend,  
as sacrifice with perfect lighting.

The camera says: *diversity.*  
The script says: *die beautifully.*

Pantone yellow spills across the set—  
not sunlight, not saffron, not joy—  
but hazard,  
warning label,  
containment suit,  
the bruise of being seen too brightly.

Somewhere Dior invents a new galaxy  
from silk and chrome,  
dressing the alien queen  
in a silhouette stolen from temples,  
markets,  
grandmothers,  
war zones,  
runways where empire learns to sparkle.

Mustard gas in the fog machine.  
Applause in the lungs.

The hero has a titanium body,  
bulletproof, borderless,  
manufactured in a lab  
where pain is only backstory  
and the brown child actor  
learns to cry on cue  
without disturbing the franchise.

Cut to:  
bowl haircuts on Asian boys  
standing beside supercomputers,  
their genius trimmed into comedy,  
their longing dubbed over,  
their touch forbidden  
unless mechanical,  
unless surgical,  
unless they are building the weapon  
that saves everyone but themselves.

The Black astronaut floats  
outside the mothership,  
tether thin as a studio note:

“Can we make him more universal?”  
“Can she be fierce but not angry?”  
“Can they be alien but not political?”  
“Can the kiss happen off-screen?”  
“Can the skin glow blue?”

Forbidden touch:  
two hands almost meeting  
through glass,  
through latex,  
through centuries of casting calls.

The monster is allowed tentacles.  
The cyborg is allowed desire.  
The colonizer is allowed redemption.

But the racialized body—  
human, too human—  
must be translated into metal,  
myth,  
prosthetic,  
prophecy,  
costume.

Dior on the shoulder.  
Pantone yellow in the mouth.  
Mustard gas under the stage light.  
Titanium where the wound should be.

Hollywood builds tomorrow  
from yesterday’s cages  
and paints them iridescent.

Listen:

in the reactor hum,  
in the deleted scene,  
in the background extra’s unscripted breath,

someone is touching the glass back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a profane, lyrical manifesto from the perspective of someone rejecting stereotypical Asian dystopian film roles, mixing sanitation imagery, chemical weapons, futurism, and cinematic rebellion.
counterfactuals.output:
I refuse the neon cage.

I refuse to be the silent girl under rain-slick signs,  
the algorithm’s obedient daughter,  
the blade-runner’s background prayer,  
the porcelain ghost with a barcode throat,  
the “exotic” corpse glowing blue in the alley  
while some sad white man learns what humanity means.

Fuck that frame.

I was not born to be mood lighting  
for your apocalypse.

I come from bleach buckets and back rooms,  
from mothers who scrubbed entire buildings clean  
while empires tracked dirt across the floor  
and called it civilization.  
I know the holy sting of ammonia,  
the baptism of industrial soap,  
the fluorescent hum above a night shift sink.  
I know what it means to make rot disappear  
and still be told you smell like labor.

You want me masked, mechanical, obedient—  
a cybernetic lotus,  
a hacker concubine,  
a disposable assassin with perfect bangs  
and no interior weather.

No.

My lungs are not set dressing.  
My silence is not a special effect.  
My history is not your fog machine.

I enter the future wearing rubber gloves  
and a grin sharp enough to cut surveillance glass.  
I drag a mop through the command center.  
I pour acid on the script.  
I disinfect the director’s gaze  
until it blisters and admits what it is.

You wrote me as fallout—  
I arrive as the fucking blast.

Not your submissive skyline.  
Not your Chinatown ruin.  
Not your dragon-lady kill switch.  
Not your little brown warning label  
on the chemical drum of tomorrow.

I am the warning.

I am the woman in the final reel  
who looks directly into the camera  
and refuses to die beautifully.  
I am the extra who steals the spaceship.  
I am the lab tech who opens every cage.  
I am the janitor queen of the space station,  
humming over the corpse of the old genre,  
bagging its clichés in black plastic,  
dragging them out back where the floodlights don’t reach.

Let the city choke on its holograms.  
Let the sterile towers sweat.  
Let the billionaires seal themselves  
inside their chrome coffins and call it progress.  
I have seen cleaner futures in a toilet bowl  
after the night crew got paid.

Bring your drones.  
Bring your militarized weather.  
Bring your gas masks, your panic sirens,  
your designer pandemics of fear.  
I will not be vapor.  
I will not be warning sign décor.  
I will not cough blood in the third act  
so a man with stubble can feel profound.

I will spit.

I will spit green fire into the projector.  
I will lace the soundtrack with riot drums.  
I will kick down the matte painting sky  
and let the real dawn crawl in, filthy and alive.

This is not representation.  
This is reclamation with a steel-toed boot.  
This is cinema after the quarantine of imagination.  
This is the future with its teeth unbleached.

I am not your dystopia.

I am the contamination in your clean myth.  
I am the unlicensed sequel.  
I am the subtitle that bites back.  
I am the body you could not flatten,  
the accent you could not domesticate,  
the face you kept casting as omen  
until I became prophecy.

Roll camera.

No, fuck that—

I roll myself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
